mercury.vtkjs.title: Mercury
mercury.vtkjs.text:
Magnetic field: The cutout slices, shows the strength of the magnetic field around Mercury. Studying the slices, particularly looking at the view from the Y-axis, shows how the solar wind is pushing the magnetic field, dragging it away from the planet and creating the tail-formation, knows as the magnetotail. The plasma wake - the region of less dense plasma on the night side of the planet, is also illustrated by the weaker magnetic field seen behind the planet, seen along the X-axis going towards -X.

IMF and Solar Wind: In the model, under B field streamlines and solar velocity streamlines, we seen two components of the solar wind illustrated. The former, showcases the interplanetary magnetic field lines (IMF), generated by the Sun, bending around the planet due to Mercury’s intrinsic magnetic field. The solar wind direction is seen by the velocity streamlines as they represent the bulk velocity of the solar wind.

Bow shock: The bow shock, the region that forms due to the solar wind meeting an obstacle in the planetary magnetic field, can be seen represented by the voxel cone that shows the particle density around Mercury. The bow shock, is an area where the plasma gets highly compressed, meaning the particles bunch up in the region. Therefore, the bow shock can be represented by the particle density.

venus.vtkjs.title: Venus
venus.vtkjs.text:
Magnetic field: As with Mercury, we have a 3-axis view of the magnetic field magnitude, represented by the sheet surfaces, around Venus. However, Venus does not have an intrinsic magnetic field like Mercury, which means that we cannot see a magnetosphere outline. Nevertheless, the solar wind does meet an obstacle in Venus’s thick atmosphere, and this interaction does induce a weak magnetic field in the ionosphere of Venus.

IMF and solar wind: Due to the lack of an intrinsic magnetic field, the solar wind is able to reach quite close to the planet. However, the thick atmosphere and induced magnetic field in the ionosphere still act as a shield, causing the IMF lines to drape over the planet, as seen in the parameter B field streamlines. The solar wind streamlines show the direction of the solar wind.

Bow shock: Because of the thick atmosphere, the solar wind cannot reach the surface of the planet, so a bow shock is formed in the interaction between Venus and the solar wind. This can be seen in the highest average particle density cone, as the particles get compressed and gather up. As opposed to Earth and Mercury, this bow shock is much closer to the planet, as there is no magnetic field stretching out from Venus.

luna.vtkjs.title: The Moon (Luna)
luna.vtkjs.text:
Magnetic field: The Moon has no global intrinsic magnetic field, and nor is one induced through interaction between the solar wind and an atmosphere, as the Moon does not have a significant atmosphere. This means that the solar wind does not meet any resistance and is able to hit the surface. Consequently, the Moon itself blocks the solar wind plasma, so on the night side of the Moon we get a region of lower density, known as a plasma wake. If the Moon sphere is removed, the Moon's role as an obstacle becomes clear in the magnetic field magnitude. Because the Moon absorbs the solar wind plasma instead of deflecting it, a cavity forms behind it, and the magnetic field is stronger along the edges of this wake, which compensates for the drop in plasma pressure.

IMF and solar wind: In contrast to Venus and Mercury, we see from the IMF lines that the presence of the Moon has a relatively small effect on the solar wind.

Bow shock: As there is no significant magnetic field, intrinsic or induced, the particles do not bunch up in any significant way, and we see no bow shock as there is no deflection.

comet2_4.vtkjs.title: Comet 2.4 AU
comet2_4.vtkjs.text:
Magnetic field: Like the Moon and Venus, a comet does not have an intrinsic magnetic field. However, unlike the Moon, it does create an obstacle for the solar wind. As the comet warms, particles and gas are released through sublimation, creating a temporary atmosphere called a coma. Because the comet releases neutral gas that is ionized into heavy ions, which are then picked up by the solar wind, the solar wind gains mass and slows down, altering its flow, a phenomenon known as mass loading. As a result, the magnetic field drapes around the comet.

IMF and solar wind: Looking at the B field lines showing the IMF, we see that they curve slightly around the comet. The velocity streamlines also show how the direction of the solar wind changes when it comes into contact with the coma, as well as the slowdown effect.

Bow shock: There is no particle density cone as a visual aid here, but we can still see the outline of the bow shock in the magnetic field magnitude sheets. Due to mass loading, the solar wind particles slow down and compress in front of the nucleus. The nucleus itself cannot be seen here because it is so small, as comet nuclei typically range from a few kilometres to tens of kilometres across.
